title: You are given K sorted linked lists. Merge them into a single sorted linked list and return its head. Explain the K-way Merge pattern, the heap-based technique, the time and space complexity, and how it maps to a real banking scenario.
shortTitle: Merge K Sorted Lists (Combine K Sorted Linked Lists into One)

s1_definition.profdef: Merge K Sorted Lists is the foundational problem of the K-way Merge pattern. We maintain a min-heap that holds one node from each list, always the smallest unmerged node across all lists. We pop the global minimum, append it to the result, and push the popped node's successor. The heap never grows beyond K entries, so each of the N total nodes is inserted and removed once, giving N log K time and K space.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India has K branch ledgers, each already sorted by transaction time. Rajesh asks for one combined statement in time order. Instead of dumping everything and re-sorting, a clerk keeps the earliest unread line from each branch on a small desk of size K, always picks the globally earliest, writes it down, and replaces it with the next line from that same branch. The desk never holds more than K lines.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep one candidate per list in a size-K min-heap and always take the global minimum.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Merge K Sorted Lists is the foundational problem of the K-way Merge pattern. We maintain a min-heap that holds one node from each list, always the smallest unmerged node across all lists. We pop the global minimum, append it to the result, and push the popped node's successor. The heap never grows beyond K entries, so each of the N total nodes is inserted and removed once, giving N log K time and K space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India has K branch ledgers, each already sorted by transaction time. Rajesh asks for one combined statement in time order. Instead of dumping everything and re-sorting, a clerk keeps the earliest unread line from each branch on a small desk of size K, always picks the globally earliest, writes it down, and replaces it with the next line from that same branch. The desk never holds more than K lines.

**One line to remember:** Keep one candidate per list in a size-K min-heap and always take the global minimum.

sections.s2_technical:
The naive approach concatenates all N nodes and sorts them, which costs N log N and ignores the fact that each list is already sorted. The K-way Merge pattern exploits the existing order so we only ever compare K current heads at a time.

The engine is a `PriorityQueue` ordered by node value. We seed it with the head of every non-empty list: `pq.add(head)` for each list. Then we loop while the heap is not empty. Each iteration calls `pq.poll()` to get the smallest node, links it to the tail of the result, and if that node has a `next`, we call `pq.add(node.next)` to bring the next candidate from the same list into contention. For example, if the heap holds nodes valued 100, 250, and 400 and we poll 100 from Rajesh's list, we immediately push 100's successor so that list stays represented.

The heap comparator must be explicit: `new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> Integer.compare(a.val, b.val))`. Senior nuance: using a dummy head node for the result list removes special-casing the first append, and the heap size is bounded by K because we only ever add a successor after removing its predecessor, so memory stays at K regardless of how many millions of nodes flow through.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India stores each account's transactions in a separate sorted list, one list per account, each already ordered by amount. The reporting team needs a single merged list of all transaction amounts across several accounts in ascending order for an audit, and the lists are far too large to collect and re-sort cheaply. This is exactly how Merge K Sorted Lists works: it produces one globally sorted stream while touching each item once.

The code defines a simple `TxnNode` linked-list node holding an integer amount and a `next` pointer, and a `StatementMergeService` exposing `mergeKLists(lists)` that returns the head of one merged sorted list. A `Demo` builds three small sorted lists representing three accounts and logs the merged order.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is three sorted lists: account one is 100, 400, 900; account two is 250, 500, 700; account three is 150, 600.

Step 1 — We seed the min-heap with the three heads 100, 250, and 150. The data lives inside the heap, which now holds exactly three nodes, one per account.

Step 2 — We poll the global minimum, 100, append it to the result, and push 100's successor 400. The heap now holds 400, 250, 150.

Step 3 — We poll 150, append it, and push its successor 600. The heap holds 400, 250, 600.

Step 4 — We poll 250, append it, push 500. The heap holds 400, 500, 600. We continue the same pop-and-replace rhythm: 400 then push 900, then 500 then push 700, then 600 (account three ends), then 700, then 900. Each account's own order is preserved because we only ever replace a node with its direct successor.

Step 5 — The heap empties and the result list is fully sorted. The merged order is produced below.

```
Oct 27, 2026 8:40:11 PM com.bank.statement.service.StatementMergeService mergeKLists
INFO: Merged 3 sorted lists into one
Oct 27, 2026 8:40:11 PM com.bank.statement.StatementMergeApplication main
INFO: Merged order: 100 150 250 400 500 600 700 900
```


sections.s6_takeaway:
Merge K Sorted Lists is the foundational problem of the K-way Merge pattern. Given K lists that are each already sorted, I merge them into one sorted list using a min-heap that holds exactly one candidate from every list. I seed the heap with each list's head, then repeatedly poll the global minimum, append it to the result, and push the successor of whatever I just polled so that list stays represented. The heap never exceeds K entries, so I touch each of the N total nodes once and the whole merge costs N log K time and K space.

The key insight I explain to an interviewer is why this beats collecting everything and sorting. Concatenating and sorting ignores the existing order and costs N log N. The heap approach uses the fact that the next global minimum can only be one of the K current heads, so I never compare more than K items at a time. A dummy head node keeps the append logic clean, and pushing a node's successor only after removing the node itself is what bounds the heap at K.

At the National Bank of India I used this to produce a single time-ordered audit statement from many per-account transaction lists that were each already sorted, without the cost of pulling everything into memory and re-sorting. I kept a size-K min-heap of the earliest unmerged amount per account and drained it into one stream. Explaining the N log K complexity, the size-K heap invariant, and the dummy-head trick is what signals to an interviewer that I understand the K-way Merge pattern rather than just reciting a merge.
